comments.author: staticdrift
comments.text:
The "500" is obviously a rhetorical number but the taxonomy is solid: input validation, address normalization, payment tokenization, tax calculation, inventory race conditions, and then the long tail of third-party scripts that can each independently take the whole flow down.

What the article gets right that most postmortems miss: the failures compound. A 0.5% failure rate at each of 40 steps is not 40 small problems, it's an 18% checkout abandonment machine.

replies.author: abandonedcart
replies.text: OP here — the compounding math was the whole reason I wrote it. Teams celebrate fixing one step from 99% to 99.5% and never multiply the chain out. The number 500 came from an actual audit spreadsheet; I stopped counting at 500 because the meeting ended.

replies.author: staticdrift
replies.text: "I stopped counting because the meeting ended" belongs on the cover of every reliability book.

comments.author: kernelpanda
comments.text: Missing from the list: the failure where everything technically works. Order goes through, payment clears, confirmation email lands — and the customer still calls support because the confirmation page redirected to the homepage before they could read the order number. Success states can fail too.

replies.author: offbyfun
replies.text: The checkout equivalent of a function that returns the right value and also deletes a file.

comments.author: formfollows
comments.text: Shameless plug since it's on topic: I maintain checkoutprobe.example.com, a synthetic-transaction tool that walks a real checkout hourly with a test card and diffs every step against a recorded baseline. Built it after an address-validation vendor silently broke us for six days. The article's point 214 (vendor changes response schema without versioning) is my origin story.
